title: Your Admiration for Others Reveals Your Core Values
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece proposes an indirect method for value-driven leaders to identify their own core values, arguing that the direct question 'what do I most value?' is too broad to produce a useful answer. Instead, the author recommends working from the outside in: asking what qualities you most admire in other people, since those admired traits tend to reflect the values a person holds most dear, even when those values aren't consciously articulated. The essay ties this technique to the broader argument that value-driven leadership depends on a small, tightly defined set of two or three core values rather than an unwieldy list of virtues. It closes by suggesting leaders can also use this same question to learn what candidates or colleagues value, particularly in interview settings.
points: The essay's key insight is methodological: reframing 'what do I value' as 'what do I admire in others' produces clearer answers by working from the outside in rather than direct introspection.
It argues explicitly for narrowing to two or three core values rather than an expansive list, treating precision as more useful than comprehensiveness.
It extends the technique beyond self-reflection into a practical interviewing tool for assessing what candidates or colleagues value.
The closing paraphrase ('Tell me what you admire, and I will tell you who you are') gives the piece a memorable, quotable close tied directly to its central technique.
quotes: They know that the clarity of a small and tight set of core values enhances their ability to be a true value-driven leader.
Asking the question, “What do I most value?“ seems like a logical place to start, but it typically doesn’t get the job done.
One way to identify the core values we hold is to examine how we see the world rather than how we see ourselves. Working from the outside in can be a game-changer.
The answer to that question normally reflects the values we hold most dear.

Good leaders often use this question to ascertain what others value as well. Asking this question in an interview setting when assessing people you don’t know well, such as job candidates, often reveals important insights.
